questions.s: Concerning the olfactory pathway, as described in Last's:
o: The first neurons are bipolar cells scattered in the neuroepithelium
Last's calls this "a unique occurrence". (Last's p. 629)
About 40 olfactory nerve filaments pass through the cribriform plate
Last's: "nearly 20" filaments. (Last's p. 629)
The filaments pierce the dura and arachnoid of the anterior cranial fossa
They pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid and pierce the meninges there. (Last's p. 629)
The olfactory tract ends in the region of the posterior perforated substance and the uncus
It ends in the region of the anterior perforated substance and the uncus. (Last's p. 629)
The second-order neurons are the mitral cells of the olfactory bulb
The filaments synapse on the mitral cells. (Last's p. 629)
The second-order neuron relays in the thalamus before reaching the cortex
The arrangement is "primitive": the second-order neuron directly activates the conscious cortex, by-passing the thalamus. (Last's p. 629)
Polysynaptic olfactory pathways activate hypothalamic and brainstem nuclei
These serve visceral and somatic effects distinct from conscious appreciation. (Last's p. 629)
Three neurons link the neuroepithelium to the olfactory cortex
Last's: trace the two neurons to the olfactory cortex. (Last's p. 629)

questions.s: Concerning the retina and optic nerve (Last's):
o: The bipolar cells of the retina are the first sensory neurons
Rods and cones activate the bipolar cells, which are the first sensory neurons. (Last's p. 629-30)
The ganglion cells lie on the choroidal surface of the retina
The rods and cones lie near the choroidal surface; the large ganglion cells lie scattered on the vitreous surface. (Last's p. 629-30)
The optic nerve fibres are the central processes of the ganglion cells
These second neurons converge to the optic disc. (Last's p. 629-30)
The temporal fibres from each retina decussate in the chiasma
The nasal fibres decussate. (Last's p. 629-30)
Crossed nasal fibres relay in layers 2, 3 and 5
Crossed nasal fibres relay in layers 1, 4 and 6; temporal (uncrossed) fibres in layers 2, 3 and 5. (Last's p. 629-30)
Temporal fibres relay in layers 2, 3 and 5
Third-order fibres leave through the retrolentiform part of the internal capsule
They then pass back in the optic radiation. (Last's p. 629-30)
Third-order fibres leave through the sublentiform part of the internal capsule
The sublentiform part carries the auditory radiation; the optic radiation is retrolentiform. (Last's p. 629-30)

questions.s: The optic tract and visual cortex:
o: The optic tract passes around the cerebral peduncle
Last's: around the midbrain (cerebral peduncle). (Last's p. 629-30)
The optic tract has three destinations
Lateral geniculate body, pretectal nuclei and superior colliculus. (Last's p. 629-30)
In the visual cortex the macula is represented anteriorly
The macula is represented posteriorly; more peripheral retina registers more anteriorly. (Last's p. 629-30)
The superior colliculus fibres mediate pupillary constriction to light
The pretectal nuclei mediate pupillary constriction; the superior colliculus serves body reflexes to light. (Last's p. 629-30)
Lies at the level of the superior colliculi
In the grey matter in the floor of the aqueduct, near the midline. (Last's p. 630)
Has an Edinger-Westphal part lying caudal to the somatic nucleus
The Edinger-Westphal (accessory oculomotor) nucleus lies cranial to the somatic nucleus. (Last's p. 630)
Gives rise to about 24 000 fibres
(Last's p. 630)
Sends fibres that traverse the brainstem with a medial convexity
The fibres traverse the brainstem with a lateral convexity, through the red nucleus and substantia nigra. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: Concerning the intracranial course of the oculomotor nerve:
o: It is attached to the medial surface of the base of the cerebral peduncle, just above the pons
(Last's p. 630)
It passes forwards between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries
(Last's p. 630)
It passes above and medial to the posterior communicating artery
It passes below and lateral to the posterior communicating artery. (Last's p. 630)
It runs just above the free margin of the tentorium
It runs just below the free margin of the tentorium cerebelli. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: The oculomotor nerve reaching the cavernous sinus:
o: Traverses the interpeduncular cistern below the floor of the third ventricle
(Last's p. 630)
Lies above the optic tract
It lies below the optic tract. (Last's p. 630)
Pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus just behind the upward bend of the internal carotid
(Last's p. 630)
Runs a tortuous course with a steep upward slope
Last's: the nerve runs straight with a gentle downward slope. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: In the cavernous sinus and orbit, the oculomotor nerve:
o: Lies in the lateral wall above the abducent nerve
(Last's p. 630)
Slants down lateral to the trochlear and ophthalmic nerves
It slants down medial to the trochlear nerve and the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal. (Last's p. 630)
Picks up sympathetic fibres from the internal carotid plexus for the smooth muscle part of levator palpebrae superioris
Loss of these fibres accounts for the partial ptosis of Horner's syndrome. (Last's p. 630)
Divides into superior and inferior divisions at the posterior pole of the cavernous sinus
It divides at the anterior pole of the sinus and immediately enters the tendinous ring. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: Within the tendinous ring and orbit:
o: The nasociliary nerve lies between the two divisions of the oculomotor nerve
(Last's p. 630)
The abducent nerve lies above the oculomotor nerve
The abducent nerve lies below it. (Last's p. 630)
Each branch enters the ocular surface of its muscle one-third of the way along
Superior rectus, medial rectus and inferior rectus. (Last's p. 630)
The Edinger-Westphal fibres run in the nerve to medial rectus
They are in the proximal part of the nerve to inferior oblique. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: Regarding the ciliary ganglion connections of the oculomotor nerve:
o: The parasympathetic fibres relay in the ciliary ganglion
(Last's p. 630)
The short ciliary nerves supply sphincter pupillae and the ciliary muscle
For pupil constriction and accommodation. (Last's p. 630)
The inferior division gives two branches only
It breaks up quickly into three branches: to medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique. (Last's p. 630)
Some afferent fibres passing through the ganglion without relay supply the conjunctiva
Last's: they supply the cornea. (Last's p. 630)
The nucleus lies at the level of the inferior colliculi
In the floor of the aqueduct near the midline. (Last's p. 630)
The nerve contains about 34 000 fibres
About 3400. (Last's p. 630)
The fibres decussate completely ventral to the aqueduct
They decussate dorsal to the aqueduct. (Last's p. 630)
The nerve emerges through the apex of the superior medullary velum
Dorsally near the midline behind the inferior colliculus. (Last's p. 630)

questions.s: Concerning the course of the trochlear nerve:
o: It clings to the under surface of the free edge of the tentorium
(Last's p. 630)
It pierces the roof of the cavernous sinus behind the oculomotor nerve
Where the free and attached margins of the tentorium cross. (Last's p. 630)
It runs forwards in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus above the third nerve
It runs below the third nerve, which then crosses it medially, so IV becomes the uppermost nerve at the anterior end of the sinus. (Last's p. 630)
It enters the superior orbital fissure within the tendinous ring
It enters lateral to the tendinous ring and passes over levator palpebrae superioris. (Last's p. 630)
Enters the ocular surface of superior oblique
It enters the orbital surface, one-third of the way along the muscle. (Last's p. 630)
Becomes the uppermost nerve at the anterior end of the cavernous sinus
Because the third nerve crosses it medially. (Last's p. 630)
Passes beneath levator palpebrae superioris in the orbit
It passes over levator palpebrae superioris. (Last's p. 630)
Runs between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries
(Last's p. 630)
The motor nucleus is in the upper pons, deep beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle
It is branchial, for first arch muscles, and so lies off centre. (Last's p. 631)
The sensory nuclei extend down to the fifth cervical segment
The spinal nucleus extends to the third cervical segment (the upper two or three segments). (Last's p. 631)
The mesencephalic nucleus lies lateral to the aqueduct in the central grey
Through the whole length of the midbrain. (Last's p. 631)
The main sensory nucleus lies medial to the motor nucleus
It lies lateral to the motor nucleus and ventral to the superior cerebellar peduncle. (Last's p. 631)

questions.s: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal:
o: Contains the cell bodies of first-order neurons
Unique: their peripheral processes pass straight through the trigeminal ganglion. (Last's p. 631)
Mediates proprioception from muscles supplied by the oculomotor, trochlear, abducent and facial nerves
And probably the hypoglossal. (Last's p. 631)
Synapses with first-order neurons from the trigeminal ganglion
Its cell bodies are themselves the first-order neurons. (Last's p. 631)
Mediates pain and temperature from the face
That is the spinal nucleus. (Last's p. 631)
Extends from the lower pons through the whole medulla
Continuous below with the gelatinous substance of the cord. (Last's p. 631)
Mediates pain and temperature
(Last's p. 631)
Is classically said to receive ophthalmic fibres in its uppermost part
The classical description is upside-down: ophthalmic fibres in the lowest part and mandibular in the uppermost. (Last's p. 631)
Is shown clinically to have a strictly divisional (V1, V2, V3) pattern
Clinical observations indicate an onion-skin pattern, working backwards from the mouth. (Last's p. 631)
The sensory root is attached to the pons well lateral and just above centre
(Last's p. 631)
The motor root emerges slightly caudal and lateral to the sensory root
It emerges slightly cranial and medial to its companion. (Last's p. 631)
The roots pass below the tentorium to the mouth of the trigeminal cave
(Last's p. 631)
The cave is a prolongation of dura over the lower border of the petrous apex
It crosses the upper border of the petrous bone near its apex. (Last's p. 631)
The dural sheath peels apart the two layers of dura flooring the middle fossa
Just lateral to where the same two layers enclose the cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 631)
The dura fuses with the pia at the posterior extremity of the ganglion
Fusion is halfway along the ganglion, the anterior extremity of the cave. (Last's p. 631)
The ophthalmic and maxillary divisions pass forwards in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus
Both are wholly sensory. (Last's p. 631)
The mandibular division passes forwards in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus before turning down
It passes straight down from the lower part of the ganglion to foramen ovale, where the motor root joins it. (Last's p. 631)
Is the nerve of the frontonasal process
(Last's p. 631)
Leaves the lower part of the trigeminal ganglion
It leaves the upper part. (Last's p. 631)
Runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus above the trochlear nerve
It runs below the trochlear nerve. (Last's p. 631)
Picks up sympathetic fibres from the cavernous plexus for dilator pupillae
(Last's p. 631)

questions.s: The tentorial (meningeal) branches of the ophthalmic nerve:
o: Arise at the anterior end of the cavernous sinus
(Last's p. 631)
Supply most of the supratentorial dura
All of it except that in the bony floor of the middle cranial fossa. (Last's p. 631)
Supply the dura of the floor of the middle cranial fossa
This is the exception: the middle fossa floor is supplied by maxillary and mandibular meningeal branches. (Last's p. 631)
Arise after the nerve divides into its three branches
They arise before it breaks into lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary. (Last's p. 631)
The lacrimal nerve passes lateral to the tendinous ring
(Last's p. 631-2)
The lacrimal nerve runs along the lower part of the lateral orbital wall
It runs along the upper part; the zygomatic nerve runs along the lower part. (Last's p. 631-2)
The frontal nerve lies between the lacrimal and trochlear nerves in the superior orbital fissure
Bunched together lateral to the tendinous ring. (Last's p. 631-2)
The frontal nerve runs below levator palpebrae superioris
It runs forward in contact with orbital periosteum above levator. (Last's p. 631-2)
The supraorbital branch is larger than the supratrochlear
A large supraorbital and a small supratrochlear branch. (Last's p. 631-2)
The supraorbital nerve supplies the frontal sinus
And the forehead except a central strip, and frontal scalp up to the vertex. (Last's p. 631-2)
The supraorbital nerve supplies the scalp back to the lambdoid suture
Up to the vertex. (Last's p. 631-2)
The supratrochlear nerve extends well beyond the hairline
It scarcely extends beyond the hairline, where the two supraorbital nerves meet. (Last's p. 631-2)
Enters the tendinous ring between the two divisions of the oculomotor nerve
(Last's p. 631-2)
Crosses below the optic nerve
It passes above the optic nerve. (Last's p. 631-2)
Runs along the medial wall below superior oblique and above medial rectus
(Last's p. 631-2)
Changes its name to posterior ethmoidal and then external nasal
It changes name to anterior ethmoidal and then external nasal. (Last's p. 631-2)
Lies in the roof of the middle and anterior ethmoidal air cells
Supplying their mucous membranes. (Last's p. 631-2)
Makes a brief appearance in the anterior cranial fossa between two layers of dura
On the cribriform plate. (Last's p. 631-2)
Supplies the posteroinferior half of the nasal septum
It supplies the anterosuperior quadrant of the lateral wall and anterosuperior half of the septum. (Last's p. 631-2)
Enters the nose through the foramen caecum
It descends through the slit alongside the crista galli. (Last's p. 631-2)
The infratrochlear nerve arises just before the nasociliary enters the anterior ethmoidal foramen
(Last's p. 631-2)
The posterior ethmoidal nerve arises distal to the infratrochlear nerve
It arises proximal to the infratrochlear. (Last's p. 631-2)
The posterior ethmoidal nerve does not reach the nasal cavity
It supplies posterior ethmoidal cells and sphenoid sinus, and is often very small or absent. (Last's p. 631-2)
The long ciliary nerves are usually four in number
Usually two. (Last's p. 631-2)
The communicating branch to the ciliary ganglion is its sensory root
Its fibres pass through the ganglion. (Last's p. 631-2)
There are usually 2-3 short ciliary nerves
There are 8-10 short ciliary nerves. (Last's p. 631-2)
The long ciliary nerves carry sympathetic fibres to dilator pupillae
Picked up by the ophthalmic nerve in the cavernous sinus. (Last's p. 631-2)
The ciliary nerves supply sensation to the conjunctiva
They supply the eye including the cornea, but not the conjunctiva. (Last's p. 631-2)
Is the nerve of the maxillary process of the first arch
(Last's p. 632)
Leaves the upper part of the trigeminal ganglion
It leaves the middle part; the ophthalmic leaves the upper part. (Last's p. 632)
Runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below the ophthalmic nerve
(Last's p. 632)
Is directed into foramen rotundum because the lateral wall fuses with dura at the medial margin of the foramen
Fusion is at the lateral margin of foramen rotundum. (Last's p. 632)

questions.s: Concerning the maxillary nerve in the pterygopalatine fossa and orbit:
o: It enters the upper part of the pterygopalatine fossa
Through foramen rotundum. (Last's p. 632)
It runs laterally for a centimetre or so in the inferior orbital fissure
And becomes the infraorbital nerve there. (Last's p. 632)
Its middle meningeal branch supplies the posterior half of the middle cranial fossa
It supplies the anterior half; the nervus spinosus supplies the posterior half. (Last's p. 632)
Its trunk runs just above the roof of the fossa
It runs below the roof of the fossa. (Last's p. 632)

questions.s: The pterygopalatine ganglion and its connections:
o: The ganglionic branches form a single stout trunk despite their plural name
It passes downwards and medially to the ganglion. (Last's p. 632-3)
Most maxillary fibres pass through the ganglion into its branches
Mingling with postganglionic fibres of the nerve of the pterygoid canal. (Last's p. 632-3)
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the anterosuperior half of the nasal septum
It supplies the posteroinferior half of the septum; the anterior ethmoidal supplies the anterosuperior half. (Last's p. 632-3)
The nasopalatine nerve supplies the gum behind the canines
It supplies the gum behind the two incisor teeth via the incisive canal. (Last's p. 632-3)
The greater palatine nerve runs between the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone and the body of the maxilla
In the greater palatine canal. (Last's p. 632-3)
The greater palatine nerve supplies all the hard palate except the incisor gum
(Last's p. 632-3)
The lesser palatine nerves supply only the oral surface of the soft palate
They supply both surfaces of the soft palate and the tonsil. (Last's p. 632-3)
The pharyngeal branch passes through the pterygoid canal
It passes back through the palatovaginal canal. (Last's p. 632-3)

questions.s: Nerve supply of the nasal walls (Last's):
o: Posterior superior lateral and medial nasal nerves supply the posterosuperior quadrant of the lateral wall and septum
They enter through the sphenopalatine foramen. (Last's p. 632-3)
Branches of the greater palatine nerve supply the posteroinferior quadrant of the lateral wall
And the adjacent floor of the nose. (Last's p. 632-3)
The pharyngeal branch supplies nasopharyngeal mucosa down to the soft palate's free border
Down to the level of the opening of the auditory tube. (Last's p. 632-3)
The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies the posterosuperior quadrant of the lateral nasal wall
It reaches the anteroinferior quadrant, including the nasolacrimal duct. (Last's p. 632-3)
Arises from the maxillary nerve in the pterygopalatine fossa
(Last's p. 633)
Runs along the upper part of the lateral wall of the orbit
It runs along the lower part; the lacrimal runs along the upper part. (Last's p. 633)
Carries postganglionic secretomotor fibres for the lacrimal gland
These go up the lateral wall to join the lacrimal nerve. (Last's p. 633)
Its zygomaticotemporal branch supplies the hairy skin of the temple
It supplies the hairless skin of the temple above the zygomatic arch; the auriculotemporal supplies the hairy scalp. (Last's p. 633)
The posterior superior alveolar nerve emerges through the pterygomaxillary fissure
As three branches. (Last's p. 633)
The posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies all roots of the three molar teeth
It supplies the molars except the anterior buccal root of the first molar. (Last's p. 633)
The middle superior alveolar nerve supplies the premolars
And the anterior buccal root of the first molar. (Last's p. 633)
The middle superior alveolar nerve arises in the infraorbital canal
It arises in the infraorbital groove; the anterior superior alveolar arises in the canal. (Last's p. 633)

questions.s: The infraorbital nerve on the face:
o: Emerges between levator labii superioris and levator anguli oris
(Last's p. 633)
Communicates with the facial nerve for proprioception from facial muscles
(Last's p. 633)
Its labial branches supply the upper lip and gum to the first premolar
To include the gum of the second premolar. (Last's p. 633)
Its nasal branches supply the whole skin of the external nose
Only a small strip of skin along the external nose. (Last's p. 633)
Leaves the inferior part of the trigeminal ganglion
(Last's p. 633)
Is joined by the motor root at foramen ovale
The motor root passes beneath the ganglion. (Last's p. 633)
Divides after about 2 cm in the infratemporal fossa
After 4 or 5 mm. (Last's p. 633)
Lies between the lower head of lateral pterygoid and tensor palati
Between the upper head of lateral pterygoid and tensor palati. (Last's p. 633)
The nervus spinosus may pass through foramen ovale
Sometimes through foramen spinosum. (Last's p. 633)
The nervus spinosus supplies the dura of the anterior half of the middle fossa
The posterior half; the maxillary supplies the anterior half. (Last's p. 633)
The nervus spinosus supplies the mastoid antrum and air cells
Passing between squamous and petrous parts of the temporal bone; it is the nerve of the first pharyngeal pouch. (Last's p. 633)
The nerve to medial pterygoid enters the superficial surface of the muscle
It sinks into the deep surface. (Last's p. 633)
Arises from the trunk before it divides
One of two trunk branches. (Last's p. 633)
Supplies tensor tympani
Via a branch near the otic ganglion. (Last's p. 633)
Supplies tensor palati
(Last's p. 633)
Relays in the otic ganglion
It only passes close to the ganglion. (Last's p. 633)

questions.s: The anterior division of the mandibular nerve:
o: Gives two nerves to the lateral pterygoid, one to each head
(Last's p. 634)
Gives a single deep temporal nerve
Two deep temporal nerves. (Last's p. 634)
Contains only one sensory branch, the buccal nerve
(Last's p. 634)
The nerve to masseter passes between the two heads of lateral pterygoid
The buccal nerve is the only nerve to pass between the two heads; the nerve to masseter passes above the upper head. (Last's p. 634)
Supplies a thumbprint area of skin below the zygomatic bone
Over the soft cheek. (Last's p. 634)
Pierces buccinator
Then supplies mucosa on its deep surface. (Last's p. 634)
Ends by supplying the vestibular gum of the mandibular premolars
It ends on the vestibular gum of the three mandibular molars. (Last's p. 634)
Is motor to buccinator
Buccinator is supplied by the facial nerve; the buccal nerve is the only sensory branch of the anterior group. (Last's p. 634)
Has two roots around the middle meningeal artery
(Last's p. 634)
Gives the major sensory supply to the mandibular joint
(Last's p. 634)
Passes in front of the neck of the mandible
It passes back deep to the neck, then curves around it. (Last's p. 634)
Runs in front of the superficial temporal vessels
Its temporal branch runs behind the superficial temporal vessels. (Last's p. 634)
Lies on medial pterygoid between the mandible and sphenomandibular ligament
(Last's p. 634)
Enters the mandibular foramen behind the inferior alveolar artery
It enters in front of the artery and vein. (Last's p. 634)
The nerve to mylohyoid pierces the sphenomandibular ligament
(Last's p. 634)
Supplies the posterior six teeth before dividing
It supplies the posterior five teeth (three molars, two premolars). (Last's p. 634)

questions.s: Terminal branches of the inferior alveolar nerve:
o: The incisive branch overlaps to the opposite central incisor
(Last's p. 634)
The mental nerve supplies the gum from the midline to the first premolar
To include the second premolar gum. (Last's p. 634)
The mental nerve carries a few otic ganglion fibres to the labial glands
(Last's p. 634)
The nerve to mylohyoid is accompanied by the submental branches of the lingual artery
By the submental branches of the facial artery and vein. (Last's p. 634)
Is joined by the chorda tympani about 2 cm below the skull base
Deep to the lower border of lateral pterygoid. (Last's p. 634)
Curves down on medial pterygoid about 1 cm behind the inferior alveolar nerve
About 1 cm in front of it. (Last's p. 634)
Passes under the free lower border of the superior constrictor
Then forward above mylohyoid. (Last's p. 634)
Passes above the submandibular duct before ascending on hyoglossus
It dips below the duct. (Last's p. 634)
Supplies only half of the floor of the mouth, the rest from the mylohyoid nerve
Last's: the lingual nerve and no other supplies all the mucous membrane of the floor of the mouth. (Last's p. 634)
Grooves the lingual plate of the mandible just below the last molar
(Last's p. 634)
Carries taste from the posterior third of the tongue
Anterior two-thirds, via chorda tympani fibres. (Last's p. 634)
Gives a gingival branch supplying the lingual gum to the midline
(Last's p. 634)
The nucleus is in the lower pons
(Last's p. 634-5)
The nerve contains about 66 000 fibres
About 6600. (Last's p. 634-5)
It emerges at the lower border of the pons above the pyramid
(Last's p. 634-5)
It pierces the dura on the clivus below the level of the jugular tubercle
Above the level of the jugular tubercle. (Last's p. 634-5)
Enters the inferior petrosal sinus at the apex of the petrous temporal bone
Then bends forwards under the petroclinoid ligament. (Last's p. 634-5)
Passes medial to the S-bend of the internal carotid in the cavernous sinus
It passes lateral to the S-bend. (Last's p. 634-5)
Enters the ocular surface of lateral rectus one-third of the way along
(Last's p. 634-5)
Enters the tendinous ring above the superior division of oculomotor
Below the inferior division. (Last's p. 634-5)
The nervus intermedius contains visceral efferent as well as afferent fibres
So "sensory root" is not entirely appropriate. (Last's p. 635)
The facial nerve contains about 70 000 fibres
About 7000. (Last's p. 635)
The facial nucleus is deep in the reticular formation of the lower pons
(Last's p. 635)
The facial nerve fibres themselves produce the bulge of the facial colliculus
It is the abducent nucleus deep to them that is responsible. (Last's p. 635)
The secretomotor nucleus is the superior salivary nucleus
Part of the visceral efferent column. (Last's p. 635)
The secretomotor nucleus is the inferior salivary nucleus
That belongs to the glossopharyngeal nerve. (Last's p. 635)
Taste fibres end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius
Which lies further laterally, mostly in the medulla. (Last's p. 635)
Cutaneous fibres from the external ear end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius
They pass to trigeminal nuclei. (Last's p. 635)

questions.s: The facial nerve at the internal acoustic meatus:
o: The nervus intermedius emerges between the pons and the inferior cerebellar peduncle
Near the vestibulocochlear nerve. (Last's p. 635)
In the meatus the facial nerve lies on the upper surface of the eighth nerve
With the nervus intermedius in between. (Last's p. 635)
The facial nerve passes into the anteroinferior quadrant of the meatus
The anterosuperior quadrant; the cochlear nerve is anteroinferior. (Last's p. 635)
The facial nerve runs below the vestibule of the internal ear
It runs above the vestibule. (Last's p. 635)

questions.s: The facial nerve in the temporal bone:
o: The geniculum is a sharp posterior bend near the middle ear
Distended by the geniculate ganglion. (Last's p. 635)
It runs in the medial wall of the middle ear below the promontory
Above the promontory and just below the bulge of the lateral semicircular canal. (Last's p. 635)
It passes deep to the aditus to the antrum
Then vertically down the facial canal. (Last's p. 635)
It emerges from the stylomastoid foramen carrying taste fibres
It has shed all nervus intermedius fibres and is purely branchial motor. (Last's p. 635)
Is a branch of the nervus intermedius
Last's: the nerve of tear secretion. (Last's p. 635-6)
Has its taste fibre cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion
For taste buds on the palate. (Last's p. 635-6)
Runs through the petrous bone at a 90 degree angle to the facial nerve
At a 45 degree slant forwards and medially. (Last's p. 635-6)
Passes above the trigeminal ganglion
It passes beneath the trigeminal ganglion in Meckel's cave. (Last's p. 635-6)
The deep petrosal nerve has its cell bodies in the superior cervical ganglion
(Last's p. 635-6)
The secretomotor fibres relay in the pterygopalatine ganglion
Taste, sympathetic and maxillary sensory fibres pass straight through. (Last's p. 635-6)
Lacrimal fibres reach the gland via the nasociliary nerve
Via the zygomatic nerve and then the lacrimal nerve. (Last's p. 635-6)
The deep petrosal nerve joins the greater petrosal at the foramen ovale
At foramen lacerum. (Last's p. 635-6)

questions.s: Branches of the facial nerve in the temporal bone:
o: Tympanic branches have their cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion
Hence herpes vesicles may appear in the external meatus and tympanic membrane. (Last's p. 636)
The chorda tympani leaves the facial nerve 6 mm below the stylomastoid foramen
6 mm above the foramen, in the facial canal. (Last's p. 636)
The chorda passes over the pars flaccida and neck of malleus
Draped by mucous membrane. (Last's p. 636)
The chorda tympani enters the middle ear through its anterior wall
It enters through the posterior wall and leaves through the anterior wall. (Last's p. 636)
Emerges at the medial end of the petrotympanic fissure
(Last's p. 636)
Grooves the medial side of the spine of the sphenoid
(Last's p. 636)
Joins the lingual nerve below the lower border of lateral pterygoid
Just above the lower border, about 2 cm beneath the skull. (Last's p. 636)
Contains fibres from both the motor root and the nervus intermedius
All its fibres belong to the nervus intermedius. (Last's p. 636)

questions.s: Extracranial branches of the facial nerve include the nerve(s) to:
o: The occipital belly of occipitofrontalis
The posterior auricular nerve. (Last's p. 636)
The posterior belly of digastric
(Last's p. 636)
Stylohyoid
(Last's p. 636)
Platysma
Via the five groups of terminal branches. (Last's p. 636)
Its first neuron is bipolar with its cell body at the base of the bony spiral lamina
The spiral (cochlear) ganglion. (Last's p. 636-7)
It pierces the dura at the anterosuperior quadrant of the internal meatus
Anteroinferior quadrant. (Last's p. 636-7)
The eighth nerve enters the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the lower border of the pons
(Last's p. 636-7)
The facial nerve lies behind the eighth nerve in the pontine cistern
The nervus intermedius and facial nerve lie in front. (Last's p. 636-7)
About 30 000 cochlear fibres relay in the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei
In the inferior cerebellar peduncle. (Last's p. 637)
Crossing fibres in the lower pons form the trapezoid body
Then ascend as the lateral lemniscus. (Last's p. 637)
Cochlear representation is largely contralateral
It is largely bilateral. (Last's p. 637)
The auditory radiation passes through the retrolentiform internal capsule
It passes through the sublentiform part. (Last's p. 637)
The inferior colliculus relays for reflex effects of sound
Through tectobulbar and tectospinal tracts. (Last's p. 637)
The medial geniculate body is a displaced hypothalamic nucleus
It is a displaced thalamic nucleus, though anatomically in the midbrain. (Last's p. 637)
The auditory cortex lies below and within the lateral sulcus
(Last's p. 637)
The pathway always has exactly three neurons
There may be more, since the trapezoid body and lateral lemniscus contain cell bodies where fibres relay. (Last's p. 637)
The maculae of utricle and saccule serve static balance
The ampullae serve kinetic balance. (Last's p. 637)
The nerve from the saccule emerges through the posterosuperior quadrant of the fundus
The posteroinferior quadrant; the posterosuperior carries the utricle, anterior and lateral ducts. (Last's p. 637)
The posterior ampullary nerve passes through the foramen singulare
(Last's p. 637)
The vestibular nerve contains about 30 000 fibres
About 18 000; the cochlear has about 30 000. (Last's p. 637)
The vestibular nuclei lie in the lateral angle of the fourth ventricle
In both pons and medulla. (Last's p. 637)
They connect with the archaeocerebellum
(Last's p. 637)
The vestibulospinal tract arises from the medial vestibular nucleus
From the lateral vestibular nucleus. (Last's p. 637)
Cortical connections relay through the lateral geniculate body
Through the medial geniculate body (bilateral thalamic relay) to the auditory region. (Last's p. 637)
Is the nerve of the third branchial arch
(Last's p. 637)
Its branchial motor fibres supply only stylopharyngeus
From the nucleus ambiguus. (Last's p. 637)
Its secretomotor fibres arise from the superior salivary nucleus
The inferior salivary nucleus, rostral to the dorsal nucleus of the vagus. (Last's p. 637)
Ordinary sensation from the tongue and pharynx enters the nucleus of the tractus solitarius
These enter the trigeminal sensory nuclei; taste and carotid afferents enter the tractus solitarius. (Last's p. 637)

questions.s: At the jugular foramen the glossopharyngeal nerve:
o: Enters the anterior compartment
(Last's p. 637)
Lies medial to the inferior petrosal sinus
It lies lateral to the sinus. (Last's p. 637)
Is separated from the vagus and accessory by a fibrous dural septum
(Last's p. 637)
Notches the inferior border of the petrous bone above the internal acoustic meatus
Just below the meatus. (Last's p. 637)
The tympanic branch passes through the tympanic canaliculus
To form the tympanic plexus. (Last's p. 637-8)
The lesser petrosal nerve may leave through the petrosal foramen
Or foramen ovale. (Last's p. 637-8)
Its pharyngeal branches are motor to the constrictors
They are afferent, not motor. (Last's p. 637-8)
It has two muscular branches
The nerve to stylopharyngeus is the only muscular branch. (Last's p. 637-8)
The nucleus ambiguus supplies all the skeletal muscle supplied by the vagus
Pharynx, upper oesophagus, larynx and palate. (Last's p. 638)
The dorsal motor nucleus lies beneath the hypoglossal trigone
It lies below the vagal trigone. (Last's p. 638)
The dorsal motor nucleus supplies cardiac and smooth muscle
Of bronchi and gut. (Last's p. 638)
The nucleus of the tractus solitarius receives the auricular branch fibres
The auricular branch skin fibres go to the trigeminal sensory nuclei. (Last's p. 638)

questions.s: The vagus at the skull base:
o: Its rootlets lie between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle
Below those of the glossopharyngeal. (Last's p. 638)
It lies lateral to the accessory nerve in the jugular foramen
It lies medial to the accessory. (Last's p. 638)
It passes behind the jugular tubercle
On the basiocciput. (Last's p. 638)
The superior ganglion lodges cell bodies of the laryngeal sensory fibres
The inferior ganglion holds all the other sensory fibres; the superior ganglion holds only meningeal and auricular. (Last's p. 638)
The pharyngeal branch passes between the internal and external carotid arteries
It carries both motor and sensory fibres. (Last's p. 638)
The superior laryngeal nerve passes superficial to the carotids
It runs deep to the carotids. (Last's p. 638)
The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane
(Last's p. 638)
The internal laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid
The external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid; the internal laryngeal is sensory to pharyngeal and laryngeal mucosa. (Last's p. 638)
The right hooks under the subclavian artery
(Last's p. 638)
The left hooks round the ligamentum arteriosum
(Last's p. 638)
They pass under the inferior constrictor just in front of the cricothyroid joint
Just behind the joint. (Last's p. 638)
They supply laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds
Below the vocal folds. (Last's p. 638)

questions.s: Vagal sensory and motor supply of the viscera:
o: Vagal branches to the gut do not carry pain fibres
Pain fibres run with sympathetic fibres. (Last's p. 638)
The vagus carries no pain from any viscera
Last's: it is sensory to the thoracic viscera (oesophagus, trachea and lungs). (Last's p. 638)
The vagal trunks enter the abdomen through the oesophageal opening
(Last's p. 638)
The vagal trunks supply the stomach from branches in the greater omentum
From branches that arise in the lesser omentum. (Last's p. 638)
The cranial root gives all its fibres to the vagus
From the nucleus ambiguus. (Last's p. 639)
The spinal root arises from the anterior horn of the upper two segments only
From the upper five or six segments (mainly 2, 3 and 4). (Last's p. 639)
Spinal accessory rootlets emerge behind the denticulate ligament
From the lateral surface of the cord. (Last's p. 639)
The spinal root passes under the upper tooth of the denticulate ligament
It passes over the upper tooth. (Last's p. 639)

questions.s: The accessory nerve in the jugular foramen and neck:
o: It passes through the lateral part of the middle compartment
(Last's p. 639)
It lies just behind the jugular bulb
The vagus and accessory lie just in front of the jugular bulb. (Last's p. 639)
It lies on the internal jugular vein over the lateral mass of the atlas
(Last's p. 639)
In the posterior triangle it descends over scalenus medius
It descends over levator scapulae. (Last's p. 639)

questions.s: The cranial root of the accessory nerve:
o: Joins the spinal root in the posterior triangle
They join hands only to pass through the jugular foramen. (Last's p. 639)
Is effectively the motor root of the vagus
To striated muscle only. (Last's p. 639)
Supplies sternocleidomastoid
The spinal root supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. (Last's p. 639)
Is analogous to the motor root of the trigeminal nerve
(Last's p. 639)
Its nucleus lies against the midline in the hypoglossal trigone
Motor and somatic. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its rootlets emerge between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle
Between pyramid and olive. (Last's p. 639-40)
It forms two roots in the canal, separated by a flange of dura that may ossify
It passes below the atlanto-occipital joint in the canal
It passes forward above the joint. (Last's p. 639-40)
Spirals behind the inferior ganglion of the vagus
Then behind and around the carotid arteries. (Last's p. 639-40)
Lies on the occipital, internal carotid and lingual arteries below digastric
On the occipital, external carotid and lingual arteries. (Last's p. 639-40)
Is covered only by the facial vein beneath the investing fascia here
Very near the skin. (Last's p. 639-40)
Passes forward on hyoglossus superficial to mylohyoid
It passes deep to mylohyoid, in the mouth. (Last's p. 639-40)
Branches before the tongue are all from C1 fibres
Joining at its exit from the skull. (Last's p. 639-40)
The meningeal branch supplies dura of the anterior cranial fossa
A ring of dura in the posterior fossa beyond the foramen magnum. (Last's p. 639-40)
The nerve to thyrohyoid arises as the nerve lies on the lingual artery
The nerve to geniohyoid arises below mylohyoid
Given off in the mouth above mylohyoid. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its upper root branches off as the hypoglossal curves between the ICA and IJV
Formerly the descendens hypoglossi. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its lower root comes from C3 and C4
From C2 and C3. (Last's p. 639-40)
It lies in the anterior wall of the carotid sheath
On the IJV under sternocleidomastoid. (Last's p. 639-40)
Sternothyroid receives C1, C2 and C3
Sternothyroid is C2, 3; sternohyoid and omohyoid C1, 2, 3. (Last's p. 639-40)
The nerves most commonly affected by trauma include I, II, III, VI and VII
Olfactory filaments are torn at the cribriform plate in anterior fossa fractures
Most deficiencies of smell are due to olfactory nerve injury
Most are due to affections of the nasal mucosa. (Last's p. 639-40)
Trochlear palsy is the commonest cranial nerve lesion
Facial nerve paralysis is the commonest. (Last's p. 639-40)

questions.s: Branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve include:
o: The carotid sinus nerve
A tympanic branch
A lingual branch
A tonsillar branch

questions.s: The facial nerve and its branches (Last's):
o: Taste from the soft palate travels in the greater petrosal nerve
Taste from the tongue via chorda tympani. (Last's p. 639-40)
Tympanic branches carry somatic sensation from the tympanic membrane
Via the tympanic plexus. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its somatic afferents end in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius
In the trigeminal sensory nuclei. (Last's p. 639-40)
The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve about 4 cm below the skull
About 2 cm. (Last's p. 639-40)
The vagal trigone overlies the dorsal motor nucleus
The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply all laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid
The accessory gives its nucleus ambiguus fibres to the vagus inside the skull
Outside the skull, at the inferior vagal ganglion. (Last's p. 639-40)
The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply mucosa above the vocal folds
Below the vocal folds. (Last's p. 639-40)
It runs superficial to the occipital and lingual arteries
It runs deep to the facial vein
It runs deep to the internal and external carotid arteries
Superficial (outside) to the arteries. (Last's p. 639-40)
Its two roots unite outside the canal
Inside the canal, above the atlanto-occipital joint. (Last's p. 639-40)
